sources.note: 'Stress typically occurs on the final syllable of a word' cited to Johnson 2014 pp. 62-64 -- a statement about Ske (seke1241), checked only to see whether Gray ever wrote a stress line for a Pentecost language; not applicable to Sowa.

sources.citation: Johnson, Kay. 2014. Static spatial expression in Ske: an Oceanic language of Vanuatu. PhD thesis, SOAS. (fn. 3-4 p. 2; fn. 20)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: online with a university library login
sources.note: Nothing about Sowa stress. Sowa appears only in footnotes: at fieldwork time only two Sowa speakers were living; 'Andrew Gray and I have made recordings of Sowa with Old Stephen at Ravsunmwel, near Waterfall village'. The thesis's stress section (pp. 62-64: final primary stress) describes Ske, not Sowa.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, "Sowa language", rev 1330806931 (2026-01-02); page created 2006-12-29 by user Andrewjgray, Phonology section added 2009-12-30 by user Tabisini (= Andrew Gray; his site andrewgray.com uses the handle tabisini). Cites Gray 2012 and Tabi Vahka 2006.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Phonology section covers consonant inventory (b d g k l m n ng p r s t v w z bw mw pw), utterance-final consonant modification, absence of prenasalisation, vowels a e i o u plus é ó, and contrastive vowel length (me 'be red' vs mee < mer 'be black'); no mention of stress or accent in any of the 85 revisions checked (first Phonology revision 334943374, the 2010-07-17 Phonology edit 373981052, and the 2012-12-09 'orthography updated to Gray (2012)' revision 527143744 all lack the words stress/accent).

sources.citation: Gray, Andrew. 2010. "Sowa language", The Languages of Pentecost Island (website pentecostisland.net; precursor of Gray 2012). Internet Archive copy 2011-07-22.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Page = ~25 basic phrases plus history (last fluent speaker died 2000; only linguist to record it alive was David Walsh, 1969 wordlist). Says explicitly: 'certain questions about the grammar and phonology of the language remain unanswered, and a fully authentic reconstruction of Sowa language will probably never be possible.' Live site is now a Sedo domain-parking page (2024-12-16 capture).

sources.citation: Lynch, John & Terry Crowley. 2001. Languages of Vanuatu: a new survey and bibliography. Pacific Linguistics 517. Canberra. sec. 3.6.3 'Seke', pp. 66-67.

sources.note: Nothing. Sowa treated as a communalect of Seke: ~20 speakers in 1972 in one village; 'Tryon (1976) includes a single wordlist for this communalect, which was collected by D.S. Walsh, which represents our sole source of information'; the authors are reluctant to treat Sowa and Seke as separate languages.

sources.citation: Tryon, D. T. 1976. New Hebrides languages: an internal classification. Pacific Linguistics C-50. Canberra. Sowa = wordlist 33, collected by D. S. Walsh (1969).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)

sources.note: Nothing for Sowa: only POC consonant/vowel correspondence tables and the 292-item wordlist; the footnotes attached to the Sowa vowel row (1 'Before u', 5 'Reflex unexplained') are not about stress. The 'in unstressed syllables' footnotes in the tables belong to other lists.

sources.access_detail: open link recorded by Glottolog or the catalog, not checked; access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: The only descriptive work Glottolog lists for Sowa (grammar sketch; covers Raga, Apma, Sowa, Ske, Sa, Bislama). Its Ske/Apma chapters may carry stress notes and its Sowa sketch is the sole place a first-hand-ish stress remark could exist; Gray's Sowa web page and Wikipedia section are its precursors and are silent.

sources.citation: Tabi Vahka, Isaiah (ed.). 2006. Tamzon Nan Dutmekan Lon Dolod Ne Sowa [First Book of Our Language which is Sowa]. Waterfall Village, Pentecost. c. 900 words and phrases with Apma glosses.

sources.note: Largest body of remembered Sowa lexicon; compiled by non-linguists with inconsistent spelling (per Gray), so unlikely to mark stress, but it is the primary local record.

sources.citation: Walsh, D. S. 1969. Sowa vocabulary list (unpublished field notes, collected mainly from John Bule Seesee of Bwaravet); published only as wordlist 33 in Tryon 1976.
